I don’t think it’s done yet.” Chapter 8 – Too Close for Comfort The Fog dragged them in silent, heavy. The trial grounds felt close today, the tight corridors of Hawkins too near, the light too dim. Wesker moved quickly, boots cracking glass beneath him as he stepped into a shadowed hallway. He needed to find the survivors before Herman decided to destroy his quota yet again. The cuff at his wrist didn’t spark today, just low hum against his skin like a warning, a quiet reminder of the threat against him. Still, he moved better than the last trial. He had spent time getting used to moving around without the aid of the virus for the first time in ages, and though he was still sluggish and the coordination had yet to balance back out, he felt more confident in his steps. The Entity could have done far worse than suppress Uroboros on him. He had seen what She did to some of the other killers when they displeased Her. In comparison, this was practically a mercy. He wouldn’t waste it. He wouldn’t be humiliated again. He found the first one crouched near a generator. Claudette. She flinched when he stepped into view but didn’t run. Not right away. She looked up at him. Not with fear. With focus. Her gaze flicked to his wrist, held for half a heartbeat too long, then up to his face. Calculating. Quiet. Like she was cataloging something. She darted left and he followed, faster than he had in days. The chase should have felt good, but each footfall jolted aches and burns that wouldn’t heal, and his prey kept losing her focus on fleeing. Her eyes had already moved on. Not to the door. Not to safety. To the cuff. By the time he cornered her, someone else was watching. Nea this time, crouched on a ledge above. No flashlight. No attempt to save. Just eyes. She didn’t even flinch when he hooked Claudette. Wesker caught her gaze, the first sharp spark of unease rippling through him, before dipping back into the hallway. The second came when Gabriel tried to dodge a hit — too early. Wesker grabbed him instead, slamming him against a crate. He saw the man’s hand move reflexively to grip at his wrist, not to pull his grip away but instead to grab at the glowing band. He threw Gabriel off hard. Harder than he needed to. The cuff pulsed once in warning, then fell quiet. What was this? They were everywhere. Elodie baited a chase and never dropped her pallet. Nea looped him in tight circles that gave her no advantage. Gabriel cut close angles, always watching. No gens popped. No real escapes. They weren’t playing to win. They were playing to observe. Wesker struck Elodie down mid-vault, just to make it stop. Her scream was real. So was the blood. But even she looked up at him with that same damned expression. Not fear. Not hatred. Curiosity. He hooked her. And left her there for the Entity to claim. The Fog pressed close, pleased in the back of his skull, but it didn’t matter. He was being studied. Not like a weapon. Not like a god. Like a specimen. He lashed out. Windows shattered. Walls cracked. His stride turned savage, all rhythm gone. The survivors scattered, finally remembering to fear him. And yet even in flight, their heads turned. Eyes flicked to the cuff. He caught Nea once — barely. She slipped the grapple with a blast mine to the face. His vision swam. A second spark pulsed red-hot through the band. His knees nearly gave. He snarled and launched himself after her, only to catch sight of Gabriel again — standing too close. Waiting. A mistake soon corrected; his pained screams delivered to the Entity with considerably more vitriol than was appropriate. By the time the final generator roared to life, two hooks had been filled and the trial grounds looked clawed through. Blood on the tiles. Scrapes in the walls. Several heavy crates cracked in the corner. And Wesker? He stood in the center of it all, breath ragged, fist trembling at his side. His coat hung heavy with blood and sweat, eyes ringed with static flashes. The cuff was quiet. But he could feel it. The station lights flickered faintly. Wesker gripped the edges of the shower room sink, riding out a wave of pain and nausea. A hum crackled through the intercom. “Subject 06-W: survivor response escalating. Notable breakdown of cooperation. Factions forming. Efficiency decline evident.” A pause, and the scratch of his pen on paper. “Collateral observation: select survivors displaying heightened interest in monitoring equipment. Engineer among them. Pattern of curiosity spreading.” “Unintended consequence. Subjects developing interest in apparatus. Will require... mitigation.” A chuckle, low and pleased. “Can’t have the lab rats chewing through the wires.” The intercom clicked silent, leaving Wesker seething in his corner, cuff humming steadily. Chapter 9 – Malfunction The Fog belched them into rust and ruin — a shattered foundry wrapped in chains and crumbling metal. Wesker hit the ground running. For a heartbeat, he looked like himself; focused, powerful, hunting. Mid stride, his body seized, snapping sideways, his momentum pitching him off-balance as the cuff flared hotter than before. He slammed shoulder-first into stone, the impact jolting dust loose in a choking cloud. The roar he let out was guttural, shredded at the edges, humiliation bleeding into rage. From then on, the trial collapsed into chaos. There was no rhythm, no strategy, no grace. Just jagged surges and violent rebounds as Wesker tried to make his body obey.
